summary: Describes COPS, a simple client and server model for supporting policy control over quality of service signaling protocols. Network devices ask a policy server for decisions and carry them out. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: A router asks a boss whether it may do something and follows the answer, like a clerk checking with a manager.

questions: how do routers get policy decisions
what is a pdp and pep
how does cops keep alive work
subtitle: A simple client and server protocol that lets network devices ask a policy server what they are allowed to do.

tldr.problem: Network devices such as RSVP routers need to apply policy, for example admission control, but the rules live on a central policy server rather than on each device.
tldr.mechanism: A device (the PEP) opens a persistent TCP connection to a policy server (the PDP), sends requests, and gets back decisions. Both sides keep shared request state, and self-identifying objects carry the data.
tldr.outcome: COPS is a Proposed Standard that is updated by RFC 4261. The RFC makes no claim that it is the only or preferred way to enforce policies.

today: RFC 2748 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 4261. It has not been obsoleted. Client-types are defined in separate extension documents.

sections.title: The Client and Server Model
sections.content:
RFC 2748 describes the Common Open Policy Service (COPS), a simple query and response protocol for exchanging policy information. The policy server is called the Policy Decision Point (PDP). Its clients are Policy Enforcement Points (PEPs). The RFC's example of a client is an RSVP router that must apply policy-based admission control to RSVP usage.

The PEP sends requests, updates and deletes. The PDP returns decisions. The RFC assumes at least one policy server in each controlled administrative domain. A PEP may also have a Local Policy Decision Point (LPDP) for local decisions, but the PDP stays the authoritative decision point and the PEP must abide by its decision.

The design goals are a simple but extensible protocol. It runs over TCP for reliable delivery, uses self-identifying objects so new kinds of clients can be added without changing COPS itself, and offers message-level security.
sections.plainLanguage: The device is the clerk and the policy server is the manager. The clerk asks questions and the manager answers, and the clerk must follow the answer.

sections.title: The COPS Header and Objects
sections.content:
Every COPS message is a common header followed by typed objects. The header holds a 4-bit Version (currently 1), 4 bits of Flags, an 8-bit Op Code, a 16-bit Client-type and a 32-bit Message Length. The only defined flag is the Solicited Message flag, 0x1. Messages MUST be aligned on 4 octet intervals.

The Client-type says which kind of policy client a message is about, and every object inside is read relative to it. Values with the most significant bit set (0x8000 to 0xFFFF) are enterprise specific. In Keep-Alive messages it MUST be 0.

Each object has a four-octet header with a two-octet length, a C-Num naming the class of information and a C-Type naming the subtype. Objects are padded to a 32-bit boundary. The sixteen object classes include Handle, Context, In and Out Interface, Reason, Decision, LPDP Decision, Error, Client Specific Information, Keep-Alive Timer, PEP Identification, Report Type, PDP Redirect Address, Last PDP Address, Accounting Timer and Message Integrity.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with a label saying what kind of message it is and how long it is. After the label come little labelled boxes of details, each padded to the same size so they are easy to find.

sections.title: Messages and How They Flow
sections.content:
There are ten messages. A PEP sends Client-Open (OPN) naming itself with a PEPID and the client-types it supports. The PDP replies with Client-Accept (CAT), which carries the keep-alive timer, or with Client-Close (CC) if it will not serve that client-type. A Client-Close may include a redirect to another PDP address and TCP port.

To get a decision, the PEP sends a Request (REQ) with a client handle and a Context object. The PDP answers with a Decision (DEC), either Install or Remove, or an Error. The first decision for a new or updated request has the solicited flag set. The PDP may also send an unsolicited decision at any time to change an installed request. The PEP can send Report State (RPT) to say whether it carried out the decision (success or failure) or to give accounting updates, and Delete Request State (DRQ) when the state is no longer applicable.

The Context object says what triggered a request: an incoming message or admission control (0x01), a resource allocation (0x02), an outgoing message (0x04) or a configuration request (0x08). With a configuration request, the PDP sends named units of configuration data in decisions and the PEP must report back on each one.

The client handle is chosen by the PEP, is opaque to the PDP and must be unique within one TCP connection and client-type. A handle MUST be explicitly deleted before it is reused.
sections.plainLanguage: The device says hello, the server says welcome, and then the device asks questions and tells the server when it is done. The server can also change its mind later and send a new answer.

sections.title: Connection, Keep-Alive and Recovery
sections.content:
COPS uses one persistent TCP connection. The PDP listens on well-known port 3288, and the PEP opens the connection. Finding the PDP is out of scope, so its location is configured or found with a service location mechanism. A PEP can talk to several PDPs when different servers handle different client-types.

The PDP's Client-Accept sets a keep-alive timer. The PEP MUST send a Keep-Alive (KA) message at a random time between 1/4 and 3/4 of the minimum timer interval, and the PDP MUST echo it back. A timer value of 0 means no extra connection checking is needed. If neither side hears anything within the interval, the connection SHOULD be considered lost.

On a lost connection the PEP SHOULD send a Client-Close with a Communication Failure error for each open client-type, then keep trying the primary PDP and any backups. While disconnected it SHOULD revert to local decisions. When it reconnects it can name the last PDP whose decisions it still caches in a Last PDP Address object. The PDP may then send a Synchronize State Request (SSQ), and the PEP re-issues its state and finishes with a Synchronize State Complete (SSC).
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides keep tapping each other to check the line is still alive. If the line goes dead, the device calls a backup server and tells it what it already knows.

sections.title: Message Integrity and Security
sections.content:
COPS has its own security in the Integrity object, which gives authentication, message integrity and replay prevention. It must be the last object in a message. It carries a 32-bit Key ID, a 32-bit sequence number and a keyed digest. The digest uses HMAC, and every implementation MUST support HMAC-MD5-96, which is HMAC-MD5 truncated to 96 bits.

Security is negotiated once per connection, in the first Client-Open and Client-Accept exchange, which uses a client-type of zero. Each side chooses the initial sequence number the other must increment by one for every later message. A wrong sequence number, unknown Key ID, bad digest or missing Integrity object leads to a Client-Close and the connection should then be dropped.

Key maintenance is out of scope, but implementations MUST at least allow keys to be configured manually. Keys should have overlapping lifetimes so that they can be rotated smoothly. As alternatives, IPsec (AH SHOULD be used for validation, ESP MAY add secrecy) or TLS MAY secure the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message carries a secret stamp that only the two sides can make, plus a counting number. A fake or replayed message gets the wrong stamp or the wrong number and is thrown out.

sections.title: Client-types and Registries
sections.content:
New policy clients are added by registering client-types, and the RFC expects each new client-type to have its own document describing its use. Values 0x0001 to 0x3FFF need Specification Required, 0x4000 to 0x7FFF are for Private Use, and 0x8000 to 0xFFFF are First Come First Served.

New object C-Num and C-Type values need IETF Consensus. New R-Types, Reason-Codes, Report-Types, Command-Codes and Error-Codes also need IETF Consensus.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who wants a new kind of client has to get a number from the official list first, so two different clients never share a number by mistake.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: 0x1 is the Solicited Message flag; others MUST be 0.

fields.name: Client-type
fields.desc: Identifies the policy client; 0 for Keep-Alive.

fields.name: Message Length
fields.desc: Size in octets of header plus all objects.
